title: Credibility Booster: MGCing the Whole Class in a Single Class Period
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. recounts a single class period in which he ran moments of genuine connection (MGCs) with every student by pulling them into the hallway individually or in small groups to discuss midterm exam results. He describes the setup — a rare 30-minute independent work stretch made possible by topic and activity familiarity — and shows, through three verbatim examples, how he paired honest feedback on performance with a personal, growth-oriented message for each student or group. The piece argues that MGCs work because they combine attention to a student's academic performance with attention to their humanity, and that doing this at scale in one sitting can recharge the teacher as much as the students. Stuart frames the exercise as a practical, repeatable model of teacher credibility in action rather than an abstract concept.
points: Stuart pairs a logistical excuse (reviewing midterm scores) with unstructured MGC time, showing how routine tasks can be repurposed into full-class relationship-building.
His three sample scripts demonstrate a consistent pattern: acknowledge the student's real performance honestly, then pivot to a specific, individualized growth ask rather than generic praise.
He deliberately randomizes which students he pulls first (not just the strugglers or high performers) to avoid signaling who he 'really' cares about.
The piece's central claim is that connecting with students' humanity and their academic progress in the same breath compounds the emotional payoff for both teacher and student.
quotes: The other day I did something that seems to have blown some fresh air right into my heart and the hearts of my students. Basically, I MGCed the whole class during a 30-minute independent work segment of the lesson.

Second, I told my students that I'd be calling them each out into the hallway, either in a small group or individually, to discuss their midterm exam results. That signaled to my class that the 30-minute time period was win-win — they got to exert a bit of autonomy in analyzing some documents on their own, and they also got to look forward to whatever mysterious things I had to say in the hallway (mwa ha ha).
There wasn't some elaborate system — I just trusted my gut and trusted that the point was getting them out there and saying things to them about their performance that were true and helpful.

Now remember: in a moment of genuine connection, all you're trying to do is make a student feel valued, known, and respected. You're making eye contact. You're speaking with conviction. You're smiling with your eyes.

And, as it turned out during this little 30-minute stretch we did the other day, one of the best ways to stoke the fires of my own heart is to take some minutes to try stoking the fires of my students.

I want you to really think about using that influence to build up the broader group this semester. When you hear folks talking down about themselves, get in there — not all bossy like, but in a "C'mon ya'll, we've got this. We can do this," kind of way.
